blocks.text: They were found on the third day, at dawn, when Vicente went downstairs to see whether the tomato had turned red. It wasn't a bang or a shout. It was a hallway silence and a white light, far too clean for a house with a cistern. Helena Valls came in last, like someone who doesn't need to walk in front to be in charge.

blocks.text: “I'm sorry,” she said to Vicente, and she seemed to mean it. “You opened a door the insurance doesn't cover. There will be no complaint filed if there are no more doors.”

blocks.text: Vicente looked at Andrés, at Aya, at the bundle, at the kitchen clock on the chair. He wanted to say something grand, and all that came out, with the dignity of a straw hat, was:
blocks.html: Vicente looked at Andrés, at Aya, at the bundle, at the kitchen clock on the chair. He wanted to say something grand, and all that came out, with the dignity of a straw hat, was:

blocks.text: “A home is a home.”
blocks.html: “A home is a home.”

blocks.text: They were taken away without handcuffs. Aya walked with her hands on her belly and Andrés beside her, measuring every corner in case there was still a shortcut. There wasn't. In the street, nobody came out. A few blinds rose a hand's width and came down again. The city, true to itself, preferred not to see the moment when three lives crossed the pavement.

blocks.text: The transfer was not to Mars. Mars, Helena said in the glider, was too far for a pregnancy this advanced and too close to the headlines. The Moon would do. The Moon was, moreover, a metaphor Nexum knew how to use: “A controlled environment, like the one humanity has already chosen on Earth.” Hearing that, Aya thought that companies sometimes speak with an involuntary honesty.

blocks.text: They took off at nightfall from a runway that didn't appear on any tourist map. Andrés, who had spent his life on a six-metre boat, felt the rocket's push as an insult to his bones. Aya, designed for ships as well, didn't get sick; even so, as she watched the Earth grow small (the Mediterranean a glint, the Mar Menor not even a dot anymore), she closed her eyes and stored the colour of the water with a precision no chip would ever have asked of her.

blocks.text: The lunar city was called Selene Norte and it was, indeed, a dome. Several domes, linked like the bubbles of a soap that never bursts. The floor was smooth, the air smelled of filters and synthetic mint, and the sky, if you looked up, was not sky: it was curved glass with the Earth hanging to one side, beautiful and uselessly far away. There were hydroponic gardens, avenues named after scientists, humanoid children and human children playing at not being told apart, and shops that sold natural light in lamps, by the hour.

blocks.text: They were housed in a white module, a “provisional family habitat”, with a little window facing a crater and a bed wider than the one in Lo Pagán. There were cameras, of course, disguised with the kind of elegance that is another form of contempt. There were doctors who smiled. There was a contract that Andrés refused to sign and that, even so, was attached to the file: precautionary custody in the interest of the unborn.

blocks.text: “You are not prisoners,” said Helena on the second day, in front of a cup of tea nobody drank. “You are protected. The girl will be born here, with every guarantee. Afterwards we'll talk about the future.”

blocks.text: “The future is not a laboratory,” said Andrés.
blocks.html: “The future is not a laboratory,” said Andrés.

blocks.text: “Every future has been one first,” she replied, and for an instant she seemed tired of her own line.
blocks.html: “Every future has been one first,” she replied, and for an instant she seemed tired of her own line.

blocks.text: Aya walked around the module, one hand on the wall, learning the different gravity, that three-quarter weight that turned every step into a doubt. Lía was growing. The belly finally rounded, and with it a watchfulness grew too: tests at odd hours, sensors stuck to the skin, questions that weren't questions. “Does the foetus dream?” “Does it respond to the parent's voice?” “Are there any signs of anomalous imprinting?” Aya answered only what was needed. At night, when the cameras didn't quite know what to do with the darkness, she sang into her belly songs that weren't in any Nexum archive: songs of the shore, of salt, of a courtyard hung with nets, which Andrés had been teaching her in a very low voice.

blocks.text: Selene Norte was beautiful in its sterile way. Walking its avenues, Aya understood that the Earth of 2060 had trained itself for this: to live under a hull, to stop missing the wind. The Moon wasn't exile. It was an enlarged portrait of what was already happening down below. The difference was the landscape, not the confinement.

blocks.text: One early morning, with no more warning than a pain both ancient and new, Aya stopped in the module corridor and said Andrés's name. She didn't shout. There was no need. He, who had slept badly since the escape, was already on his feet.

blocks.text: They took her to the medical block, a place of soft lights and gloved hands. Helena appeared at the back, not as a surgeon, but as the company's witness. Andrés didn't throw her out: he had no power to throw anyone out on the Moon. He stood at the head of the bed, held Aya's hand and talked to her about the Mar Menor, about the mornings when the water looks like pewter, about the flamingos, about coffee without sugar, so that her cultivated body would have somewhere to return to between one contraction and the next.

blocks.text: Lía was born at the start of the lunar day, which is a manner of speaking, because the lunar day is a decision made by clocks. She didn't cry right away. She looked. She had Andrés's eyes, dark and patient, and under the skin of her left wrist a blue light, barely visible, like a thought that had turned into a glow. The doctor held his breath. Helena took a step forward. Aya, sweating, exhausted, more human than any report, drew the baby to her chest, and then Lía cried, a short, clear cry, and the whole module seemed, for a second, like a home.

blocks.text: Andrés touched his daughter's cheek with a trembling, salty finger, and laughed, and his eyes filled again.

blocks.text: “Hello, Lía,” he said, and the name, which Aya had kept since August, could finally be spoken.

blocks.text: Helena, from the doorway, looked at the blue light on the wrist and didn't say “product”. She said, more quietly, almost against her will:

blocks.text: “Welcome.”

blocks.text: Then she went out, and in the corridor she recovered the stride of someone who has to write a report. The report would record: full-term birth, stable phenotype, residual luminous pigmentation on the wrist, hybrid origin confirmed. The report wouldn't record that the mother had sung, or that the father still smelled, in memory, of esparto grass and old petrol, or that the baby, falling asleep, closed her glow like someone closing a door from the inside, not to shut herself in, but to rest.

blocks.text: In the hours that followed, the medical block wanted to take the baby away “just for a moment” for a sensor panel. Aya refused with a softness that allowed no negotiation. Lía would stay at her breast, under the same light, with the same air, with the same voice. A young nurse, perhaps trained less in protocols than in instinct, brought them a blanket that wasn't entirely white, and that, in Selene Norte, amounted to a small and memorable act of rebellion.

blocks.text: Aya, with Lía in her arms, looked through the little window at the crater and, beyond it, at the Earth. She searched for the place where the Mar Menor was and couldn't find it. It didn't matter. The place was in her chest, in the tiny weight of her daughter, in Andrés's hand on her shoulder.

blocks.text: In Selene Norte, the domes went on with their impeccable routine. A girl of two worlds had been born, and the world, below and above, still didn't know which law she would deserve.
